Every Saturday morning, a small blue van stops at the edge of Rampur village. Its sides open like a cupboard, and inside are shelves full of books — stories, comics, science magazines and books in Hindi, English and Marathi. This is the village’s “library on wheels”, started three years ago by a retired schoolteacher, Mrs. Kulkarni.

At first, only a handful of children came. Many parents felt that reading storybooks was a waste of time when there was farm work to be done. Mrs. Kulkarni did not argue. Instead, she began reading aloud under the neem tree. Soon, mothers and grandparents stopped to listen too. Within a year, more than eighty people had library cards, and the oldest member was a seventy-year-old farmer who had just learnt to read.

Teachers in the village school say that children who borrow books regularly now write better and ask more questions in class. Mrs. Kulkarni smiles when she hears this. “Books do not ask whether you are rich or poor, young or old,” she says. “They only ask you to open them.”

Read the passage and answer the questions.
1. Every year, millions of Indians donate blood, yet hospitals often report shortages. One unit of donated blood can help up to three patients, because it can be separated into red cells, plasma and platelets.
2. A healthy person between 18 and 65 years of age who weighs at least 45 kg can usually donate blood. The process takes about ten minutes, and the body replaces the lost fluid within a day. Red cells are replaced in a few weeks.
3. Blood cannot be manufactured in a factory. It must come from donors. Platelets last only about five days in storage, which is why regular donation is needed rather than large drives once a year.
4. Many myths stop people from donating — that it causes weakness, or that it is painful. In reality, donors feel only a small pinch, and they are given juice and a short rest afterwards.
5. Schools and colleges can help by spreading awareness. Students under 18 cannot donate, but they can encourage family members and help organise camps.
